First, are we saying there's a difference between restricting and censoring? For instance, as you note, recipes for weaponry - and I don't just mean 3D-printed guns or homemade Fight Club napalm, but the design specs for creating a nuke. I would say there is a difference between labeling some information as restricted and the notion of strong censorship, though, in which an idea is made completely verboten, unspeakable and ideally unthinkable. Two of the very few places I see that happening (with a good case being made that it's logical and reasonable to censor) is in the fields of human genetic tampering and artificial intelligence - in the former, people are rightly very concerned about human experimentation and Gattaca-style issues, and in the latter, you have big names coming out saying that AI is a very possible apocalypse scenario that needs to be safeguarded against. Even then, only very specific parts of the overall research are being targeted, and it's not as though technology is advanced enough for this stuff to be more than speculative anyway. Point is that there's strong argument as to why it's logical and reasonable to censor here, and on a humanity-wide scale. I don't know that I personally find the arguments compelling enough, but stuff like that is probably as close an answer as I can think of to your original question.

The two examples you gave, genetic engineering and artificial intelligence, they are both too valuable to humankind to be banned, just like quantum physic, we all know the risks of potential misuses that may lead to disastrous consequences, but we are still willing to take the chance, preferably with great cautions.
